newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Northern chief Dostum puts planes into Afghan war.
newsitem.headline: Northern chief Dostum puts planes into Afghan war.

text.p: Northern Afghan chief Abdul Rashid Dostum used warplanes to bomb positions of the Taleban militia on Saturday after his forces came under attack in the remote northwest, a spokesman for a member of Dostum's alliance said.
Rockets also hit the airport in the capital Kabul, held for the past month by the Taleban, on Saturday, witnesses said. Taleban fighters denied the rockets struck within the perimeter.
It was not immediately clear who fired the rockets or whether they had caused any significant damage.

"(Dostum) jets from the north went over this morning," he said," Dr Abdullah, spokesman for former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood told reporters in the town of Jabal os-Siraj, 70 km (45 miles) north of Kabul.

The Taleban, opening a second front after weeks of trying to mollify Dostum, attacked Dostum's forces in Badghis province on Thursday. There was no independent word on claims they had overrun districts in northwestern province of Badghis and in neighbouring Faryab province.
Taleban-controlled Radio Afghanistan, renamed Voice of Sharia (Islamic law), said the offensive was continuing.

"The so-called Defence Council of Afghanistan wanted to disrupt the peaceful life of people in Badghis province and by doing so wanted to continue their growing pressure on people," official Radio Afghanistan said on Saturday.
The Defence Council was set up two weeks ago formally linking Dostum and of Ahmad Shah Masood.

"Therefore they had concentrated their defeated militias on the frontier of Badghis province but the devoted heroes of the Islamic Army dealt a decisive blow against the band of evil and corruption," the radio said.
"As a result of the pounding operations of the Islamic Army districts of Ghormach and Morghab in Badghis and Quaysar district in Faryab province were completely cleared of the nnemy."
"The advance of the Islamic Army towards Faryab province is continuing," it concluded.
Afghan watchers in Kabul confirmed there had been fighting but said it was unclear how much ground the Taleban had made.
Abdullah said Masood was not concerned about the new front.
"We are not worried, the Taleban can open as many new fronts as it wishes," he said.
Taleban fighters barred journalists and most travellers from using the westernmost road running north of Kabul to the front line, saying they were clearing the area of arms.
Refugees fleeing the area in trucks said the western plains were largely calm on Saturday and said there were few people in local villages left to disarm.
An unidentified aircraft flew over Kabul early on Saturday and dropped a bomb. It was not clear where the bomb landed in the heavily war-damaged city.

Masood fighters in Bagram, a few kilometres (miles) north of the front line, said two Dostum planes had bombed Taleban forces defending the De Sabz pass on the easternmost road running north from Kabul.
The Taleban offensive in the remote northwest appeared to reflect growing confidence they could handle two foes at once.

A mullah at Kabul's main mosque berated Dostum as "a former communist and a criminal" on Friday, a day after the Taleban administration said it had evidence Dostum forces were fighting alongside those of Masood on its northern front.

Until now the Taleban have been anxious to avoid Dostum entering the conflict and have taken pains to emphasise they have no quarrel with him despite his communist past and the more liberal climate of provinces under his control.
The attack, which began on Thursday, appeared to dash hopes of a ceasefire in Afghanistan's civil war. The conflict has also alarmed its neighbours and other regional powers.

Iran has said it will host a regional conference on the issue on Tuesday, gathering Russia, India, Pakistan, China, Saudi Arabia and Central Asian states. The European Union and the Organisation of the Islamic Conference are also invited.
